title: Container Security Reviews
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of container security reviews.
Choose and interpret a suitable Docker example connected to container security reviews.
Predict an expected result and verify it using observable evidence in a controlled environment.

content.intro: This lesson covers Container Security Reviews. You will connect the named subtopics from the supplied Docker curriculum to a small, observable example. Work through the visual first, then use the example to form a prediction and check it against the actual behavior.
content.why_it_matters: Treat an image and its runtime settings as part of the security boundary. Use maintained image bases, non-root execution where possible, minimal capabilities, constrained mounts and networks, secret-safe build mechanisms, and vulnerability/component review. Docker daemon access itself is privileged. Learning container security reviews helps you make deployment behavior explicit and repeatable instead of relying on a command that happened to work on one machine.

content_blocks.title: Layered container security controls
content_blocks.caption: Image trust, user identity, capabilities, filesystem, network, and daemon access are separate review points.

items.title: Reviewing Dockerfiles
items.text: For reviewing dockerfiles, name the relevant Docker object, setting, or operational step; predict its effect; and capture evidence from a controlled test or inspection command. Relate the result back to container security reviews rather than assuming that a successful command proves the wider system is correct.

items.title: Reviewing Compose configuration
items.text: Compose declares services and shared resources together. Use `docker compose config` to inspect the resolved model before starting or deploying it.

items.title: Reviewing privileges and mounts
items.text: Reduce privileges to the minimum required, then run the intended application workflow to catch permission assumptions; container hardening is platform- and workload-dependent.

items.title: Checking secret exposure
items.text: A secret needs a restricted path from its source to the process that needs it. Avoid putting it in images, normal build arguments, source control, or diagnostic output.

items.title: Creating a release security checklist

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with the supplied example for container security reviews. Before running it, state what you expect to happen. Compare the real output with that prediction, then change one variable or setting in a disposable lab to test the boundary of the idea. If a command is not supported on your operating system or installed Docker version, consult the linked official reference and record the actual version rather than guessing.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Container Security Reviews
content_blocks.expected_output: On a compatible Linux-container environment the process runs as UID/GID 10001 with a read-only root filesystem and reduced privileges.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run in a local test Docker environment; options differ by OS/runtime, and the intended app may need additional specific permissions.
content_blocks.reset_steps: The container is removed at exit; no named storage is created.
content_blocks.safety_note: Security-hardening example. Verify compatibility and required capabilities rather than copying flags blindly to production.

content_blocks.title: Practical checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Keep this lesson in draft while reviewing: Container Security Reviews. Capture the command/configuration, expected and actual result, one failure or edge case, and cleanup performed. This course does not award XP from content files; CodeLeaf backend rules remain authoritative.

task: Apply container security reviews to a small local case. Record the configuration or command, expected result, observed result, one limitation/edge case, and how you verified the result.
hints: Begin with read-only inspection commands and identify the active Docker context before any mutating action.
Use a disposable name, local test image, and synthetic data; change one thing at a time.
If the outcome differs, preserve the exact error and logs, check the official reference for your installed version, and document the verified fix.
expected_output: On a compatible Linux-container environment the process runs as UID/GID 10001 with a read-only root filesystem and reduced privileges.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming that a successful start means the application is ready.
common_mistakes.why: A container can start while its dependent service is unavailable or the application is failing after startup.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect health/status and logs; add a meaningful health check or retry strategy where appropriate.

common_mistakes.problem: Keeping required data only in the container writable layer.
common_mistakes.why: Replacing the container can discard that layer and its application state.
common_mistakes.fix: Select a named volume or an external storage system, then rehearse a restore.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a command without checking context, target, or permissions.
common_mistakes.why: Docker commands affect the active endpoint and can change host resources or publish services.
common_mistakes.fix: Check `docker context show`, use an isolated lab, make the smallest change, and verify the resulting state.
